questions.question: Given the knowledge base consisting of the two sentences (1) B₁,₁ ⇔ (P₁,₂ ∨ P₂,₁) and (2) ¬B₁,₁, after converting all sentences to CNF and applying a single resolution step, which of the following clauses is correctly derived?
questions.explanation:
Converting (1) to CNF yields (¬B₁,₁ ∨ P₁,₂ ∨ P₂,₁) ∧ (B₁,₁ ∨ ¬P₁,₂) ∧ (B₁,₁ ∨ ¬P₂,₁) (see conversion steps on [Page 4]). Clause (2) is ¬B₁,₁. Resolving ¬B₁,₁ with (¬B₁,₁ ∨ P₁,₂ ∨ P₂,₁) removes the complementary literals, leaving the resolvent P₁,₂ ∨ P₂,₁, which corresponds to option B.

questions.question: Which most general unifier (MGU) makes the literals parent(X, john) and parent(mary, Y) identical?
questions.explanation:
Unification requires substituting X with mary to match the first argument and Y with john to match the second argument, giving the MGU {X/mary, Y/john}. This follows the unification procedure described on [Page 4] (unification, 14:19).

questions.question: Using Generalized Modus Ponens, which conclusion can be derived from the Horn clause ¬hasKey(X) ∨ canOpen(Y, X) and the fact hasKey(k1)?
questions.explanation:
The clause is equivalent to hasKey(X) ⇒ canOpen(Y, X). Instantiating X with k1 and using the fact hasKey(k1) allows us to infer canOpen(Y, k1) by Generalized Modus Ponens (see page 4, “Generalized Modus Ponens, 14:20”).

questions.question: In a propositional knowledge base in CNF, which inference rule should be applied when a clause contains the literals L and ¬L (in any two different clauses)?
questions.explanation:
The presence of complementary literals L and ¬L allows the Resolution rule to combine the two clauses, eliminating the pair and producing a resolvent. This is the core of the resolution algorithm described on [Page 180] and [Page 196].

questions.question: A robot planning system maintains a set of Horn clauses representing its actions. Which reasoning strategy is most appropriate for deriving all possible new facts from the current knowledge base without a specific goal in mind?
questions.explanation: Forward chaining repeatedly applies inference rules (e.g., Modus Ponens) to a Horn KB to generate all derivable facts, which matches the description of forward chaining on [Page 4] (14:21). Backward chaining, by contrast, works from a goal backward.
